equivalents.note: The Tibetan keeps the word as a transcription; the same syllables open its reading of the rāga name Paṭamañjarī (pa Ta ha'i snye ma, song 1), and the commentary here writes rnga pa Ta ha, 'the paṭaha drum' (cp.19.m2).

The Tibetan has the generic 'great drum' (rnga bo che), the same word its commentary uses for the kettledrum (dundubhi, cp.19.m2) and its name for the rāga Bhairavī in song 12, so it does not single out the mādala.
The Tibetan line has 'great drum' (rnga chen) and puts its sound in the sky (mkha' la), which the Bengali line does not say but Munidatta's comment does (ākāśe, cp.19.m2).

The Tibetan renders surata by its parts as 'great delight' (shin tu dga' ba), not a word for lovemaking, and reads the -pasaṅga of suraapasaṅge as a companion (grogs) with whom the poet keeps company ('grogs).
The Tibetan renders raeṇi pohāa together as 'dawn broke' (nam langs, here spelled nams langs), so 'night' survives only as the first syllable of 'dawn'.
The Tibetan reads saṅga as a person, 'the companion of great bliss' (bde ba chen po'i grogs), as its verse reads the -pasaṅga of cp.19.4a.
The Tibetan quotes the cry 'may it be victorious' (rgyal bar gyur cig) as a lemma and then lists sgra, 'sound', as the first of the omens, breaking up the Sanskrit compound.
The commentary has rnga bo che, the standard equivalent and the word the verse uses for the mādala (cp.19.1a), where the refrain has rnga chen; the śabda of dundubhiśabda is not rendered separately.
The Tibetan has 'nonconceptual' (rnam par mi rtog pa) where the Sanskrit has the conceptual thought (vikalpa) of mind, wind and the rest, reversing the sense, perhaps from a reading nirvikalpa.

The verse Tibetan (cp.19.3a) has no word for jāma, reading ahāriu as 'food' (kha zas), but the commentary cites a lemma skye ba'i, 'of birth', at the point where Shastri's Sanskrit has jayam iti, and explains it as the faults of birth and destruction.

The Tibetan renders 'the fruit of the marriage with Ḍombī' as 'the fruit of the Ḍombī bride' (bag ma), and in the next sentence gives vivāha by sense as 'her going is to be destroyed' ('gro ba gzhom par bya), reading vi-vāha as stopping the flow.

The Tibetan has 'ocean of wisdom' (ye shes kyi rgya mtsho) instead of the standard 'wisdom seal' (ye shes kyi phyag rgya) it uses in cp.19.m5, as if reading samudra for mudrā, or through a slip for rgya.
The commentary cites the lemma raeṇī as nam, 'night', and glosses its passing as the clearing (sangs pa) of the darkness of the afflictions.
As in the verse (cp.19.4a), surata is 'great delight', and abhiṣvaṅga is rendered mngon par 'grogs pa, 'keeping close company'.
The Tibetan has 'the fire of life' (srog gi me) where the quoted verse has jīvānila, 'the wind of life', as if reading anala, 'fire', for anila, 'wind'.

equivalents.wylie: shin du mngon par dga' ba
equivalents.lemma: shin tu mngon par dga' ba
equivalents.note: Here the commentary writes shin du mngon par dga' ba, adding mngon par, and renders abhiṣvaṅga as mngon par chags pa, 'attachment', rather than 'keeping company' as in cp.19.m4.
The verse Tibetan (cp.19.5a) has no word for yogi, reading jo joi as gang gang, 'whoever, whoever', like Munidatta's ye ye; the commentary has the standard rnal 'byor pa for his yoginaḥ.

questions: karanda (cp.19.1b): not matched. The Tibetan line names one instrument, khar rnga, 'bronze drum' (already matched to kasala), for the pair karaṇḍa and kaśālā, and makes mind and wind the ones who sound it (sgrogs par byed) rather than the instruments themselves; no word is left for karaṇḍa, and the commentary does not take it up.

prabhasvara (cp.19.m5): not matched. The Tibetan renders prakṛtiprabhāsvarapariśuddhāvadhūtikā as rang bzhin yongs su dag pa'i a wa d+hU tI pa, 'the naturally purified avadhūtī', with no 'od gsal; either its manuscript lacked prabhāsvara here or the translators dropped it. The term is matched in cp.19.m4.

yogi (cp.19.5a) and janma (cp.19.3a): the verse Tibetan has no word for either, so I have given the commentary's renderings instead (rnal 'byor pa'i in cp.19.m5, skye ba'i in cp.19.m3). Should these be recorded against the verse lines as well?
pataha (cp.19.m2): no separate answer. The commentary writes rnga pa Ta ha, which the text-wide search for the clear pa Ta ha (cp.19.1a) will find.
